The Red Baron. Manfred von Richthofen, the most famous combat pilot of World War One, who recorded eighty confirmed kills, far exceeding most rivals and making him the highest-scoring pilot of the entire war. He painted his fighter bright red, making himself easily visible but giving him a powerful psychological advantage over his opponents. Richthofen flew the Fokker Doctor-One triplane, a nimble aircraft suited to his aggressive dogfighting tactics. On April twenty-first, nineteen eighteen, near the war's end, he was shot down by Canadian or Australian ground fire near Amiens and killed. His autobiography, The Red Fighter Pilot, became a bestseller and ensured his posthumous status as a legend. Richthofen represented the romanticism and honor of early aerial combat before dogfighting tactics became more mechanical and impersonal. Beyond his own flying prowess, he commanded a fighter squadron, demonstrating leadership and mentoring of younger pilots. Eddie Rickenbacker was America's answer to Richthofen's combat prowess, competing for kill records against pilots like him. Jimmy Doolittle, another American pilot who survived World War One, went on to greater fame, representing aviation's evolution beyond the age that Richthofen defined.
